items.caption: C(4,2) = C(3,1) + C(3,2)
items.text: The highlighted entry is the sum of the two directly above it, which is Pascal’s rule read off the array instead of out of the formula. Every interior entry is built the same way, so the whole triangle can be generated from its edges of 1s without evaluating a single factorial. items.caption: One polynomial through the counts
items.text: For k = 2 the descending-product form gives C(x, 2) = x(x − 1)/2, a parabola in x. At x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 it passes through 0, 0, 1, 3, 6 — the number of ways to choose 2 items from x. Between and beyond those points the same formula still returns a value: 15/8 at x = 5/2, and 1 at x = −1. Those values count nothing; they are what the algebraic definition adds, and what Newton’s generalized binomial theorem uses.

items.caption: C(7,2) = C(7,5) = 21
items.text: The two highlighted entries sit at mirrored positions in the same row and hold the same value, which is the identity C(n,k) = C(n,n−k) drawn rather than proved. Choosing which 2 of 7 items to take is the same act as choosing which 5 to leave, and the array makes that restatement visible as a reflection. items.caption: Every pick, sorted by its b's
items.text: Multiplying out (a + b)(a + b)(a + b) means taking a or b from each of the three factors, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 picks in all. Sort the picks by how many b’s they take: one pick has none, three have one, three have two, one has three. Each column is a set of positions chosen for the b’s, so its size is C(3, k), and all its picks multiply to the same a³⁻ᵏbᵏ — which is why that binomial coefficient becomes the term’s coefficient.

items.caption: Four items into boxes of 2, 1 and 1
items.text: The coefficient of x₁²x₂x₃ in (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)⁴ counts the ways to hand the 4 factors to three labelled groups: two factors give x₁, one gives x₂, one gives x₃. Filling Box A with 2 of the 4 items, then Box B and Box C with 1 each, gives 4!/(2!·1!·1!) = 12 partitions, so the term is 12x₁²x₂x₃. Try other group sizes on the

items.caption: Three choices, then two
items.text: Choose a shirt, then trousers. Each of the 3 shirts opens its own branch, and every branch splits the same 2 ways, so the tree ends in 3 × 2 = 6 leaves — one for each outfit, each reached by exactly one path. Add a third step with k options and every leaf would split k ways again: that repeated splitting is why the counts multiply.

items.text: Every one of the 81 assignments of 4 items to 3 cells is enumerated here, and not one of them leaves all three cells with a single item — there are simply not enough cells to go round. That is the pigeonhole principle as an exhaustive check rather than an argument: the crowded cell is present in all 81 cases, which is why the conclusion needs no construction. items.caption: The overlap, counted twice
items.text: The example from the text, region by region: 11 students take only French, 8 only Spanish, 7 both, and 4 neither. The 18 French students include the 7, and so do the 15 Spanish students, so 18 + 15 = 33 counts those 7 twice. Subtracting |F ∩ S| once gives 26, the same as adding the three inner regions directly.

items.caption: Permutations of 1, 2, 3 and the sets Aᵢ
items.text: A permutation is in Aᵢ when element i stays in position i, so the last column is how many of the sets it belongs to. The identity is in all three, three permutations are in exactly one, and two are in none. Adding the column gives 6 = 3·2!, the sum of the |Aᵢ|, and the complementary form removes everything that is in at least one set, leaving the 2 derangements.

items.caption: Three guests, three hats
items.text: Guests A, B and C each checked a hat, and the six rows are every order the hats can come back in. A red circle marks a guest who got their own hat back. Four orders return at least one hat correctly; only B C A and C A B leave every guest holding someone else’s hat — the two derangements, so !3 = 2. The alternating sum under the table is the formula for n = 3: start from all 3! orders and correct for the ones that fix a place.
